items.t: Abbott vs. Medtronic: Which Dividend Stock Pays You More in 10 Years?
sum: - Medtronic finished splitting off its MiniMed diabetes business on Oct. 15, and Abbott plans to spin off its Nutrition business by the end of 2027.
- Medtronic has the higher yield, 2.9% against 2.5%, but Abbott has raised its dividend 9.4% a year over its last five fiscal years, against 4.1% at Medtronic.
- Both dividends are well covered, taking 64% of free cash flow at Abbott and 60% at Medtronic over the latest twelve months, and 54% and 58% on analysts’ estimates.
- Medtronic reports on Nov. 24, its first results since the split-off.

Medtronic (MDT) finished splitting off its diabetes business on Oct. 15. It swapped its remaining stake in MiniMed for about 55 million of its own shares. Six days later, Abbott Laboratories (ABT) said it plans to spin off its Nutrition business, the home of Similac and Ensure, by the end of 2027.

So, both dividends will soon come from leaner companies. Medtronic pays the bigger check today, a 2.9% yield against Abbott’s 2.5%. But Abbott’s dividend has grown more than twice as fast. So, which one pays you more over the next 10 years?

sum: Medtronic (NYSE: MDT) reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 adjusted earnings per share of $1.45, surpassing the analyst consensus estimate of $1.39 by 4.32 percent.

The medical technology giant also posted quarterly sales of $9.756 billion, beating the consensus estimate of $9.545 billion. Sales rose 13.73 percent from $8.578 billion in the same period last year, while earnings per share increased 15.08 percent from $1.26 per share.

The divergence between revenue growth and earnings growth highlights improved operational efficiency or margin expansion during the quarter. While revenue grew 13.73 percent, adjusted EPS grew at a faster clip of 15.08 percent. This suggests that cost management or favorable mix shifts contributed to profitability beyond simple volume growth.

Furthermore, the company beat both revenue and earnings estimates, indicating stronger-than-expected demand or execution in its core markets. The 2.21 percent beat on sales and 4.32 percent beat on EPS suggest robust underlying business momentum. Analysts noted that non-GAAP gross margin expanded to 65.2%, topping the consensus estimate of 64.8%.

Cardiovascular sales grew 19.5%, or 18.9% organically, to $3.927 billion. Cardiac Rhythm Management sales rose 15%, while Cardiac Ablation Solutions surged 88%. Neuroscience revenue climbed 10.3%, or 9.3% organically, to $2.678 billion. Cranial and Spinal Technologies grew 13%, including low-20s growth in enabling technology. Altaviva also helped drive 15% growth in Pelvic Health.

Medical Surgical sales increased 10%, or 10.2% organically, to $2.279 billion. Surgical sales rose 9%, while Acute Care & Monitoring grew 14%. Diabetes revenue increased 16.9%, or 14.9% organically, to $843 million.

Medtronic raised its fiscal 2027 adjusted earnings guidance from $5.90-$6 per share to $5.94-$6 per share. The new range compares with the $5.95 consensus estimate. The company also lifted its organic revenue growth forecast to 7.25% to 7.75%, up from its previous range of 6.75% to 7.25%.

Medtronic stock expands neurovascular portfolio with new guidewire
sum: Medtronic has expanded its neurovascular portfolio with the launch of the Aristotle Mini Guidewire, following U.S. Food and Drug Administration 510(k) clearance in August. The company announced the launch on Monday, November 9, in a Medtronic business and regional news release.

The new guidewire is designed to help physicians navigate smaller, more distal vessels in procedures including middle meningeal artery embolization for chronic subdural hematoma. Medtronic said the device complements its Onyx liquid embolic system and other neurovascular technologies.

Aristotle Mini is compatible with 0.013-inch inner-diameter microcatheter workflows. The company also said the guidewire may support procedures involving arteriovenous malformations and dural arteriovenous fistulas, where access to small vessels can be critical.

Medtronic plans an initial commercial rollout, with broader availability after early physician experience. That timing gives investors a near-term product milestone but does not yet provide a sales forecast, procedure target or revenue contribution.

sum: Medtronic reported past six month results from its SPYRAL AFFIRM post approval study, showing statistically significant blood pressure reductions with the Symplicity Spyral renal denervation system across diverse US patient groups and no increase in antihypertensive medications.

The FDA has already cleared a labeling update for the Symplicity Spyral Multi Electrode Renal Denervation Catheter, adding data in isolated systolic hypertension, chronic kidney disease up to stage 3b, and type 2 diabetes. This broadens the real world clinical evidence base Medtronic can point to with physicians.
Now the focus shifts to how Medtronic's broader investment narrative could be influenced by stronger SPYRAL AFFIRM renal denervation data.

To own Medtronic, you need to be comfortable with a large device maker that grows by rolling out new therapies while managing product complexity and recalls. According to LunaRodas, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the bigger narrative is about multiple product engines carrying mid single digit revenue expansion and steady earnings growth rather than rapid acceleration.

Recent FDA enforcement reports around the OmniaSecure defibrillator lead and CareLink SmartSync programmer keep product quality and regulatory execution in focus. These recalls look contained in volume but still lean into the key near term risk that quality issues distract management and absorb capital just as newer growth drivers such as cardiac ablation and renal denervation seek wider adoption.

The enforcement report tied to the OmniaSecure Model 3930M ventricular lead is probably the most relevant disclosure for investors watching Medtronic right now. It touches the cardiac rhythm management franchise that management previously highlighted as a flagship contributor with durable growth, so product reliability in this area matters for the broader story.

sum: - Medtronic launched an exchange offer to split off most of MiniMed, its former diabetes unit.
- A neutral look at the mechanics, motives and risks for MDT owners.
- Medtronic opened an exchange offer that lets its owners of the stock swap ordinary shares for stock of MiniMed, the diabetes business it floated earlier this year.

Medtronic plc (NYSE:MDT) Healthcare Medtronic PLC (NYSE:MDT) 101.80 USD -3.040 2.900% Last Updated at: 2026-11-06T21:11:00Z , one of the largest medical technology companies in the world, has begun what it describes as the final stage of separating its diabetes franchise. The company opened a voluntary exchange offer that allows owners of its ordinary shares to trade them for common stock of MiniMed Group, Inc. (Nasdaq:MMED) MMED (NASDAQ:MMED) , the business that went public earlier this year and in which Medtronic still keeps a large majority stake.

At the centre of the story is a split-off, a corporate maneuver in which a parent company offers its own owners of the stock the chance to exchange parent shares for shares of a subsidiary. Medtronic said it would offer enough MiniMed stock to move a notable share of that business out of its hands, and that if demand is strong it can add the whole remainder of its keeping to the pool.

The offer is voluntary, which means a shareholder who takes no action keeps exactly what was held before and is not affected by the transaction in any direct way. The company framed the launch as a statement of confidence in MiniMed as a standalone enterprise.

The headline feature is a discount. Medtronic said tendering owners would receive MiniMed stock worth a bit more than the Medtronic stock they hand over, with the gap described as a notable discount on the MiniMed side. In plain terms, a participant receives slightly more value in MiniMed shares per US currency of Medtronic shares, measured at the averaged prices.

Employee Stock Purchase Plans and the Burden of Substantiation: Tax Court Rejects Taxpayer Claim That ESPP Gains Were Included in Form W-2 Wages
sum: Moiseshyn v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-114, November 4, 2026

In Moiseshyn v. Commissioner, the United States Tax Court addressed a bit of confusion the taxpayers encountered when handling employee stock plan dispositions. The taxpayers believed they could defeat an IRS deficiency determination for omitted securities gains by asserting that the capital income was already embedded within Box 1 compensation on Form W-2, or at least that their employer’s guidance was so confusing their error should be excused. Writing for the Court, Judge Fung sustained the Internal Revenue Service’s deficiency determination regarding unreported securities gain from an Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP), as well as omitted dividend and Treasury interest income.

The decision underscores the rigorous substantiation requirements imposed on taxpayers under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 61 and Tax Court Rule 142(a). For CPAs and Enrolled Agents (EAs), Moiseshyn serves as a critical reminder that third-party informational disclaimers—such as brokerage guides stating that ESPP income is “usually” included in Box 1—do not constitute probative evidence of actual wage inclusion, nor do they shift the burden of proof back to the Commissioner.

The taxpayers, Anthony J. Moiseshyn and Mai Moiseshyn, were pro se petitioners residing in California during the tax year at issue. From 1999 through his retirement in 2025, Mr. Moiseshyn served as a principal sales representative for Medtronic PLC (Medtronic). As a fringe benefit of his employment, Mr. Moiseshyn participated in the Medtronic Employee Stock Purchase Plan, an employee plan administered through Fidelity Brokerage Services LLC (Fidelity). Under the terms of the ESPP, eligible full-time employees could elect to contribute between 2% and 10% of eligible compensation to acquire Medtronic stock at an 85% discount relative to fair market value on quarterly purchase dates.

Between March 31, 2015, and March 31, 2020, Mr. Moiseshyn acquired numerous shares of Medtronic stock through Fidelity, establishing an aggregate cost basis of $57,498.37. On June 2, 2021, Mr. Moiseshyn liquidated these shares for total proceeds of $99,805.16, generating an aggregate gain of $42,306.79.

Medtronic stock gains focus as ablation data support growth
sum: Medtronic reported positive real-world registry results for two cardiac ablation systems on October 22, 2026, with findings presented at the Asia Pacific Heart Rhythm Society meeting. The company's Medtronic press release covered the Affera Mapping and Ablation System with the Sphere-9 catheter and the PulseSelect pulsed field ablation system.

Medtronic stock traded at 88.44 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 12:07 CET on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. Investors are weighing the clinical evidence alongside the company's portfolio shift toward cardiovascular, neuroscience and surgical businesses following the completed MiniMed separation.

The global APEX registry analysis included 1,050 patients with atrial fibrillation treated with Sphere-9 and the Affera system at 28 sites. Medtronic reported a 1.1% major complication rate, with no acute kidney injury, severe coronary spasm or phrenic nerve injury. Major complication rates did not differ significantly between first-time and repeat ablation procedures.

The REAL PULSE registry covered 1,160 atrial fibrillation patients treated with PulseSelect at 38 global sites. The analysis recorded a 100% acute success rate and an acute major complication rate of 0.09%, according to the company.

A separate European APEX analysis evaluated Sphere-9 in 46 patients undergoing treatment for sustained ventricular tachycardia. Acute success reached 87%, while estimated freedom from ventricular tachycardia recurrence at six months was 75%. Six major complications were reported in four patients.

Medtronic said the results reinforce confidence in the safety and performance of its ablation technologies. Khaldoun Tarakji, the company's vice president of science, research and technology for electrophysiology therapies, said the findings reflected encouraging physician response and real-world evidence across a broad range of arrhythmias. Felicia Kurz, vice president and general manager of Cardiac Ablation Solutions, said the company would continue developing care that is safe, effective and efficient.
The findings strengthen the clinical case for Medtronic's electrophysiology portfolio, but registry results alone do not establish a revenue forecast.

items.t: The 10 Best Dividend Stocks for 2026
sum: What should investors look for when it comes to choosing the best dividend stocks to buy today?

At Morningstar, we think that the best dividend stocks aren’t simply the highest dividend stocks or the top-performing dividend stocks. We suggest that investors look beyond a stock’s yield and short-term performance—instead, choose stocks with durable dividends and buy those when they’re undervalued.

“Tempting as they might be, the stock market’s juiciest yields are often illusory,” explains Dan Lefkovitz, strategist for Morningstar Indexes. “High dividend yields are often found in risky sectors, industries, and companies.” And as a result, such high dividend yields can’t always be maintained.
Investors seeking durable dividends should instead focus on companies with management teams that support their dividend strategies and favor companies with competitive advantages, or economic moats.
“Moats signify a durable competitive advantage. Moats protect profits from competition. And profits fund dividends,” reminds Lefkovitz.
Investors looking for good dividend stocks to buy might consider adding undervalued dividend stocks with economic moats to their portfolios.

Intuitive Surgical's Moat Is Getting Stronger. Is This the Closest Thing to a 'Forever' Stock?
sum: You may have come into contact with Intuitive Surgical (ISRG -3.35%) without even realizing it -- for example, if you've had a hernia repair or another type of minimally invasive surgery. Intuitive Surgical is the maker of the world's leading surgical robot, the Da Vinci system, which assists surgeons across many common procedures. This dominance has helped the company deliver earnings growth and stock performance over time.

Intuitive Surgical has an extremely strong moat, or competitive advantage, and it may be getting even stronger. This means the company may not face the threat of competition any time soon -- and this is excellent news for the earnings picture and for investors. Is Intuitive Surgical the closest thing to a "forever" stock? Let's find out.

So, first, let's consider the company's flagship product and its path so far. Intuitive Surgical offers the Da Vinci platform in four different versions, from a value-oriented product to the latest update, the Da Vinci 5. This latest Da Vinci includes more than 150 design innovations and 10,000x more computing power than the previous release. The new features offer strengths in areas like surgeon autonomy and operating room workflows. In the first quarter of this year, Da Vinci 5 placements totaled 232 -- that's up from 147 in the year-earlier period, showing momentum for this new product.

Intuitive Surgical's moat is particularly strong for a few reasons. Most surgeons have trained on the Da Vinci system, so we could imagine that they would prefer using this system, one they know well. The Da Vinci also represents a million-dollar purchase for hospitals, so once a hospital has committed to the platform, it likely will aim to stick with it to amortize the investment. Finally, a Da Vinci is deeply integrated into operating room operations, making it time-consuming and costly to switch to an alternate platform.

Now it might surprise you when I say that a new entrant to the market actually makes Intuitive Surgical's moat stronger. Medtronic won clearance late last year for its Hugo system for urologic surgical procedures. Importantly, Medtronic has emphasized that the Hugo may represent another "choice" for these surgeries -- so the company isn't positioning its product as a better option than the Da Vinci.

This sector-wide pressure compounded the lingering market skepticism surrounding Medtronic’s long-term growth trajectory following its recent earnings report. Although the company delivered strong fiscal fourth-quarter results that beat top-line expectations, its forward-looking guidance for fiscal year 2027 fell short of the consensus estimate, prompting several analysts to trim their target prices. Furthermore, research updates during the month scaled back growth projections for the company's highly anticipated Symplicity Spyral Renal Denervation System, revising its expected annual revenue growth contribution downward. Investors remain cautious about persistent operational headwinds, including margin compression from recent legal payments and ongoing tariff pressures, which offset the optimism surrounding the company's product pipeline and surgical robotics expansion.

sum: Whether you believe there's a bubble in tech or are just worried about rising valuations in the stock market, there's ample reason to want to reduce risk right now. By diversifying into dividend stocks with stable businesses, you can make your portfolio less vulnerable in the event of a market crash or correction in the near future.

That stability is evident in its top line, which has been steadily growing. sum: Medtronic PLC (MDT) moved down by 3.14%. The Healthcare Services & Equipment sector is down by 1.36%. The company underperformed the industry. Top 3 stocks by turnover in the sector: Unitedhealth Group Inc (UNH) up 0.42%; GE Healthcare Technologies Inc (GEHC) down 12.39%; Boston Scientific Corp (BSX) down 3.32%.

Medtronic (MDT) experienced a notable decline in its share price on April 29, 2026, reflecting significant intraday volatility. This downturn appears to be largely influenced by a confluence of negative analyst sentiment and lingering concerns over a recent cybersecurity incident.

Several financial analysts adjusted their outlook for Medtronic in the preceding days, contributing to a cautious investor environment. Jefferies, for instance, lowered its price target for MDT from $108 to $95 on April 23, 2026, while maintaining a Hold rating. This revision was partly attributed to the timing of an initial public offering (IPO) related to its Minimed unit and associated one-time expenses, leading to reduced earnings per share estimates for fiscal years 2026 and 2027. Similarly, UBS also decreased its price target for Medtronic from $104 to $90, citing the IPO's impact on earnings. Other firms, including Truist Financial and Mizuho, also reduced their price targets, and Weiss Ratings downgraded the stock from a "buy" to a "hold." These widespread analyst revisions can significantly influence investor perception and lead to selling pressure.

Adding to the negative sentiment was the disclosure on April 24, 2026, that Medtronic had identified unauthorized access to some of its information technology systems. While the company stated that its products, patient safety, manufacturing, and financial reporting systems were not impacted, and that it did not expect a material financial effect, such breaches often introduce uncertainty and concern among investors regarding potential reputational damage, remediation costs, and future data security risks. The market's reaction suggests that these concerns weighed on the stock despite the company's reassurances.
Furthermore, on the day of the price change, Medtronic's stock touched a new 52-week low.

Brain-Computer Interface Stocks: 14 Supply Chain Plays Before the Neuralink IPO
sum: Scientists have already completed a full digital map of a microscopic roundworm called C. elegans — every neuron, every connection. Last year, they did it for a marine worm with three times as many neurons. It’s the kind of milestone that doesn’t make the front page of the Wall Street Journal, but it should.
Because if you can map a worm’s brain, the next question becomes: how long until a mouse? How long until a human? And what technologies have to scale for that to happen?

When I started thinking about that question seriously, I did what 28 years on a trading desk teaches you to do: I flipped to the supply chain. Who makes the chips this math runs on. Who builds the electron microscopes that image the tissue. Who sequences the proteins. Who makes the memory that’s now the real bottleneck.
Most of those companies are already public. Several of them are trading at market caps that don’t remotely reflect what happens if the underlying thesis is right.

Meanwhile the headline version of this story — the one retail investors hear every day — is Elon Musk’s Neuralink. Twelve patients implanted. A $9 billion private valuation. Reports of a confidential filing toward an IPO.

And in January 2026, OpenAI led a $252 million funding round into Merge Labs, a brain-computer interface startup co-founded by Sam Altman, valuing the company at $850 million. Altman himself did not invest personal capital. The structure raised eyebrows in the financial press given the circular dynamic of OpenAI investing in a company Altman co-founded — but the substantive signal is that one of the most strategically positioned investors in artificial intelligence has decided brain-computer interfaces are worth a nine-figure check.
Retail will pile into Neuralink and Merge Labs when they go public. Fine. The valuations on those listings will already price in years of growth.
